Clustering spatial transcriptomics data

Data Lab for ALSF

2026

Objectives

  • Perform dimensionality reduction (PCA and UMAP) and graph-based clustering on Visium data
  • Use the Banksy package to perform spatially-aware dimensionality reduction and clustering
  • Compare clusters calculated with and without spatial information

Introduction

In this notebook, we’ll cluster expression data from a mouse sample with osteosarcoma lung metastases from Reinecke et al. (2025). This sample was processed using second-generation Visium technology and quantified with Space Ranger 2.1.1. We have already processed this dataset for you, including filtering out low quality spots (SpotSweeper removed 20 low-quality spots) and normalization, which you can see in this notebook: https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/training-modules/blob/master/spatial/setup/osteo/prepare-osteo-data.Rmd.

As we have discussed, Visium spatial transcriptomics data does not quantify expression at the single-cell level, but rather each Visium spot captures the combined expression of 1-10 cells. This means that when we perform clustering on Visium data, we are actually clustering spots with similar transcriptional profiles, not individual cells.

Also unlike single-cell data, we now have an additional consideration of spatial information. In many cases (but not all!), it’s reasonable to assume that nearby spots will tend to have more similar expression to one another than to distant spots. We can therefore incorporate each spot’s physical position in the tissue alongside its expression profile during clustering, which may help to approximate spatial domains.

In this notebook, we’ll explore complementary approaches: first running expression-based dimensionality reduction and clustering just as we would for single-cell data, and then performing the same analyses using the Banksy package. Banksy (sometimes also stylized as BANKSY) offers a spatially-aware dimensionality reduction and clustering approach that augments each spot’s expression with information from its spatial neighborhood.

Set up

To begin, we’ll load the packages we’ll use throughout this notebook.

# The main class we use for spatial transcriptomic data
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(SpatialExperiment)
})
Warning: replacing previous import 'S4Arrays::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' by
'DelayedArray::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' when loading 'SummarizedExperiment'
# To support plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Set ggplot2 theme
theme_set(theme_bw())

We’ll set a seed for reproducibility, since we’ll be running UMAP and clustering.

set.seed(2026)

Directories and files

The pre-processed SPE object for this sample is stored in a sample-specific subdirectory of data/osteo, organized by GEO sample ID.

# define sample id we'll be analyzing
sample_id <- "GSM8478586"

# data directory for this sample
data_dir <- file.path("data/osteo", sample_id, "normalized")

normalized_rds <- file.path(data_dir, "osteo_normalized_spe.rds")

We’ll also define the path for outputting clusters. To save space, we’ll conclude by exporting a TSV with the clusters we calculate in this notebook (along with other per-spot metadata).

cluster_tsv <- file.path(data_dir, "osteo_clusters.tsv")

Import

Let’s start by reading in the pre-processed SPE object:

spe <- readr::read_rds(normalized_rds)

Before working with this SPE, let’s get familiar with it. We’ll first print the SPE to review its contents, including the number of spots and genes and what assays are available.

We’ll also create a plot of the H&E image to orient ourselves to the tissue before diving into clustering, adjusting the styling of the plot to our preferences. We’ll refer back to it throughout the notebook to help interpret the spatial patterns we find.

# define H&E plot for general use in notebook
he_plot <- ggspavis::plotVisium(spe, spots = FALSE, zoom = TRUE) +
  # add styling to match other panels
  theme(
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, 0.1, 0)
    ),
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "black", linewidth = 0.3)
  )

he_plot

This image clearly shows regions of tumor cells amid the lung parenchyma, which appears less dense because of the lung’s alveolar spaces.

Let’s also get a sense of the RNA counts here by plotting some of the QC statistics that were calculated for you, including the total UMIs (sum) and number of unique detected genes (detected). Note that these plots use an upper limit on the color scale to be able to see lower value spots more clearly.

total_plot <- ggspavis::plotCoords(spe, annotate = "sum", point_size = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    # cap scale at 20,000; all value above this will be shown as 20,000
    limits = c(0, 20000),
    # tell the scales to "squish" to the limit specified above, where
    # oob stands for "out of bounds" handling
    oob = scales::oob_squish,
    # fun with color scales!
    option = "plasma"
  )
detected_plot <- ggspavis::plotCoords(
  spe,
  annotate = "detected",
  point_size = 1
) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    # cap scale at 10,000
    limits = c(0, 10000),
    oob = scales::oob_squish,
    option = "plasma"
  )
total_plot + detected_plot

There is clearly more RNA expression in the tumor regions than in the parenchyma, which makes sense biologically. Tumor cells are highly proliferative and transcriptionally active. In addition, the lower density of parenchymal tissue makes for fewer cells per spot, and less overall expression.

This plot also illustrates why local QC filtering thresholds are preferable to global ones for heterogeneous tissue samples like this. Specifically, the parenchymal spots have lower UMI and gene counts not because they are low quality, but because of the alveolar architecture of lung tissue itself. A global threshold would not distinguish between a genuinely low-quality spot and a spot that overlies sparse tissue, and would have ended up preferentially removing parenchymal spots. For a Visium experiment, we want to retain much of the spatial context, including the contrast between tumor and parenchymal regions, and using local QC thresholds allows us to do so.

Dimension reduction and clustering

The first clustering analysis we’ll perform will look analogous to single-cell post-processing. After that, we’ll compare to clustering with the Banksy approach to see how including spatial information influences cluster detection.

Expression-only analysis

In this section, we’ll apply the same dimensionality reduction and clustering workflow we would use for single-cell data, treating each spot’s expression profile as the unit of analysis without any spatial information. This serves as a useful baseline for comparison when we later apply a spatially-aware approach.

Again, remember that we are working at the spot level. This means clusters will represent groups of similar spots, each of which may include multiple nearby cells.

When calculating PCA, we often prefer to reduce the number of genes to only the most highly variable ones, which will both speed up calculations and ensure stronger signal. To do this, we’ll start by modeling per-gene expression variance with scran::modelGeneVar(), which separates each gene’s variation into biological and technical components, using the observed relationship between mean expression and technical variation. We’ll then use these modeling results to select the 2000 genes with the highest biological variation (these are our high-variance genes, aka HVGs). Finally, we’ll perform PCA that considers just these genes with scater::runPCA().

# model gene variance
gene_variance <- scran::modelGeneVar(spe)

# calculate the top 2000 HVGs
hvg_vector <- scran::getTopHVGs(gene_variance, n = 2000)

# calculate PCE using the top HVGs, saving back to the SPE object
spe <- scater::runPCA(spe, subset_row = hvg_vector)

Next, we will perform graph-based clustering using scran::clusterCells(), which calculates clusters using the bluster package under the hood.

We’ll use Jaccard weighting and the Louvain algorithm, specifying k = 20 nearest neighbors. We’ll also save these clustering parameters as cluster_params so we can reuse the same settings when running spatially-aware clustering later.

But first, one caveat: it’s worth noting that the choice of k and clustering algorithm are important analytical decisions (as well as other parameters like resolution, which we are leaving at its default value of 1 here). In your own research, we do recommend taking some time to explore parameter space when clustering, which you can learn more about in the the scRNA-seq-advanced training module’s clustering evaluation exercise.

# define clustering parameters
cluster_params <- bluster::NNGraphParam(
  k = 20,
  cluster.fun = "louvain",
  type = "jaccard"
)

# perform clustering and save to SPE colData
colData(spe)$cluster_nonspatial <- scran::clusterCells(
  spe,
  use.dimred = "PCA",
  BLUSPARAM = cluster_params
)

We’ll also calculate a UMAP for visualization using scater::runUMAP().

spe <- scater::runUMAP(spe)

Let’s visualize our results so far by plotting the UMAP and spatial coordinate plots, each colored by cluster with the same color palette. We’ll also include the H&E image for reference.

# define UMAP plot
umap_nonspatial <- scater::plotUMAP(
  spe,
  color_by = "cluster_nonspatial",
  point_size = 0.5
) +
  # set custom palette and legend title
  scale_color_brewer(
    name = "Non-spatial cluster",
    palette = "Dark2"
  ) +
  # ensure more visible points in legend
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 1.5))
  ) +
  # remove axis scales from umap plot
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )

# define coordinates plot
coords_nonspatial <- ggspavis::plotCoords(
  spe,
  annotate = "cluster_nonspatial",
  point_size = 1
) +
  # set custom palette and legend title
  scale_color_brewer(
    name = "Non-spatial cluster",
    palette = "Dark2"
  )

# combine plots with patchwork
umap_nonspatial + coords_nonspatial + he_plot

This has resulted in five clusters. How do you think these compare to regions in the H&E? What patterns do you see, for example between tumor and parenchymal regions?

Spatially-aware clustering with Banksy

Banksy (Singhal et al. 2024) is a package for spatially-aware dimensionality reduction and clustering. These spatially-aware clusters can also serve as a first step towards tissue domain identification.

This method rests on the assumption that spots in the same tissue domain tend not only to share similar expression profiles, but also tend to be surrounded by spots with similar expression. In other words, nearby spots are likely to be transcriptionally similar. Banksy leverages this insight by incorporating neighborhood information into the PCA itself. Performing clustering on this spatially-aware PCA allows Banksy to identify clusters with both distinct expression and tissue domain structure.

The Banksy algorithm works in three steps:

  1. Compute the Banksy matrix with Banksy::computeBanksy().

For each spot, Banksy::computeBanksy() averages expression across its k_geom nearest spatial neighbors to create a neighborhood expression profile, stored as the H0 assay. Optionally, Banksy::computeBanksy() can also compute an Azimuthal Gabor Filter (AGF), which captures directional expression gradients that can help resolve finer structure at domain boundaries. When AGF is turned on, a second Banksy matrix is stored as the H1 assay (the 0 and 1 in these assay names indicate if AGF is off or on, respectively).

  1. Run Banksy PCA with Banksy::runBanksyPCA().

Banksy::runBanksyPCA() first creates a single matrix that is a weighted combination of the normalized expression in logcounts and the Banksy neighborhood matrix (H0 or H0 and H1 if AGF is on). To combine these matrices, Banksy introduces the lambda parameter. lambda ranges from 0 – 1 and controls how much weight is given to the Banksy neighborhood information matrix relative to logcounts expression, where a value of 0 considers only logcounts expression. The Banksy authors recommend a value of lambda = 0.2 for Visium spot data, as described in this Banksy vignette on parameter selection.

Banksy then performs PCA using this combined matrix as the input.

  1. Perform graph-based clustering.

Once the PCA is calculated, it can be used for a variety of downstream tasks, including clustering and UMAP calculation. In this notebook, we’ll use scran and scater tools for these steps, but we will also point out that Banksy includes wrapper functions for these calculations, which can be useful if you are evaluating multiple Banksy parameters at once.

In this notebook, we’ll run Banksy in two configurations — without AGF and with AGF — and compare the results.

Before we get started, we have to modify our SPE object. When calculating the spatially-aware matrix and the PCA, Banksy uses all genes present in the SPE; it does not subset to only the most variable genes. To ensure a fair comparison between clustering approaches, we will subset the SPE to the HVGs that we identified before running Banksy and save it to a new variable hvg_spe. We’ll use this SPE object for the rest of the notebook.

# subset the SPE to contain only HVGs
hvg_spe <- spe[hvg_vector, ]

Running Banksy without AGF

We’ll start by computing the Banksy matrix without AGF. As noted above, lambda = 0.2 is a commonly used starting point for Visium spot data; this value means roughly 80% of the signal in the combined matrix comes from each spot’s own expression and 20% comes from its neighborhood. We’ll use k_geom = 18 spatial neighbors for the neighborhood averaging, which is also the recommended starting point for Visium spot data.

# define parameters recommended for Visium
lambda <- 0.2
k_geom <- 18

# calculate the Banksy matrix without AGF
hvg_spe <- Banksy::computeBanksy(
  hvg_spe,
  assay_name = "logcounts",
  k_geom = k_geom
)

Now, we can use Banksy::runBanksyPCA(), which combines logcounts and H0 into a single matrix weighted by lambda and then runs PCA on it.

# calculate PCA within Banksy
hvg_spe <- Banksy::runBanksyPCA(hvg_spe, lambda = lambda)

# show the SPE

The new PCA that Banksy has calculated is named PCA_M0_lam0.2: M0 indicates that AGF was not used, and lam0.2 records the lambda value. Banksy generates these names automatically, making it easy to track different reduced dimension calculations when comparing multiple runs.

To keep the workflow consistent with what we did above, we’ll use scater and scran directly for calculating UMAPs, plotting, and clustering. We’ll also reuse the same cluster_params object defined earlier when we performed non-spatial clustering to ensure a direct comparison.

# define PCA and UMAP names for bookkeeping
pca_name <- "PCA_M0_lam0.2"
umap_name <- "UMAP_banksy_nonagf"

# calculate UMAP
hvg_spe <- scater::runUMAP(
  hvg_spe,
  dimred = pca_name,
  name = umap_name
)

# perform clustering
colData(hvg_spe)$cluster_banksy_nonagf <- scran::clusterCells(
  hvg_spe,
  use.dimred = pca_name,
  BLUSPARAM = cluster_params
)

Let’s visualize this initial set of Banksy clusters alongside the H&E, just as we did for the expression-only results.

# define UMAP plot
umap_banksky_nonagf <- scater::plotReducedDim(
  hvg_spe,
  dimred = umap_name,
  color_by = "cluster_banksy_nonagf",
  point_size = 0.5
) +
  # set custom palette and legend title
  scale_color_brewer(
    name = "Banksy cluster",
    palette = "Set1"
  ) +
  # ensure more visible points in legend
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 1.5))
  ) +
  # remove axis scales from umap plot
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )

# define coordinates plot
coords_banksky_nonagf <- ggspavis::plotCoords(
  hvg_spe,
  annotate = "cluster_banksy_nonagf",
  point_size = 1
) +
  # set custom palette and legend title
  scale_color_brewer(
    name = "Banksy cluster",
    palette = "Set1"
  )

# combine plots using patchwork
umap_banksky_nonagf + coords_banksky_nonagf + he_plot

How do these clusters compare to the expression-only results? What differences do you see between these results, both in terms of the UMAP and the coordinates plot?

Running Banksy with AGF

Now we’ll re-run Banksy::computeBanksy() with AGF enabled (compute_agf = TRUE). As introduced above, AGF captures directional expression gradients and can help Banksy detect finer spatial structure at the boundaries between tissue domains.

When AGF is enabled, k_geom takes a vector of two values rather than a single one. The first value is used for the neighborhood averaging step, as before. The second value, which is usually larger, provides the broader spatial context needed for the AGF gradient calculation.

As suggested in the Banksy documentation, we’ll use k_geom = c(18, 30) for Visium spot data: 18 spots will be used for the neighborhood averaging and 30 spots will be used for the AGF calculation.

# specify 18 neighbors for neighbor averaging, and 30 neighbors for AGF
k_geom <- c(18, 30)

# turn on compute_agf
hvg_spe <- Banksy::computeBanksy(
  hvg_spe,
  assay_name = "logcounts",
  compute_agf = TRUE,
  k_geom = k_geom
)

The SPE now contains an additional assay, H1, which stores the AGF-based neighborhood expression profile. Note that if you re-run Banksy::computeBanksy() with different parameters, the new object will only include the new H0 and H1, as well the BANKSY_params entry from that run. We are saving back to the existing variable, so we are losing our previous results.

If you want to preserve results from multiple runs, you will need to keep this in mind and store each set of results separately.

Now we can run Banksy::runBanksyPCA() with use_agf = TRUE. With this argument, the function concatenates H0 and H1 when constructing the combined expression-plus-neighborhood matrix that will be input to PCA.

# use_agf tells Banksy to incorporate both the H0 and H1 assays, as well as logcounts expression
hvg_spe <- Banksy::runBanksyPCA(hvg_spe, lambda = lambda, use_agf = TRUE)

The new PCA is named PCA_M1_lam0.2, where M1 indicates that AGF was used (compared to M0 from the without-AGF run), and lam0.2 records the lambda value. We’ll now proceed to calculate the UMAP embeddings and clusters using the same cluster_params that we have been using previously.

# define reducedDim names
pca_name <- "PCA_M1_lam0.2"
umap_name <- "UMAP_banksy_agf"

# Calculate UMAP
hvg_spe <- scater::runUMAP(
  hvg_spe,
  dimred = pca_name,
  name = umap_name
)

# Perform clustering
colData(hvg_spe)$cluster_banksy_agf <- scran::clusterCells(
  hvg_spe,
  use.dimred = pca_name,
  BLUSPARAM = cluster_params
)

Now let’s visualize all three sets of results side-by-side: expression-only, Banksy without AGF, and Banksy with AGF.

wrap_plots(plot_list, nrow = 2)

What differences do you see between Banksy clusters with and without AGF? Do you think AGF captured boundaries more cleanly as advertised? Next, how do the spatially-informed clusters overall compare to non-spatial clusters?

We can get a more quantitative view of how the clustering approaches relate to one another with a heatmap comparing Banksy clusters (rows) to non-spatial clusters (columns). For this heatmap, we’ll specifically use the Banksy AGF clusters. We’ll also normalize each column by the total number of spots in the given non-spatial cluster; each tile will be colored by the proportion of spots in the non-spatial cluster.

# table of cells in each cluster
clusters_tab <- table(
  colData(hvg_spe)$cluster_nonspatial,
  colData(hvg_spe)$cluster_banksy_agf
)

# Use proportions() to normalize rows (margin = 1) to sum to 1
clusters_tab <- proportions(clusters_tab, margin = 1)

# plot heatmap:
# non-spatial clusters are columns, and Banksy with AGF clusters are rows
pheatmap::pheatmap(
  clusters_tab,
  # turn off heatmap hierarchical cluster for easier viewing
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  cluster_rows = FALSE,
  # show cluster type with the labels
  labels_row = paste0("Non", levels(hvg_spe$cluster_nonspatial)),
  labels_col = paste0("AGF", levels(hvg_spe$cluster_banksy_agf))
)

The heatmap shows non-spatial clusters labeled with “Non” and Banksy AGF clusters labeled with “AGF” and how they relate to one another. For example, non-spatial clusters labeled above as Non3 and Non5 contain tumor-rich spots, and each each appear to be split across several Banksy AGF clusters. On the other hand, cluster AGF1 does not correspond strongly to any single non-spatial cluster, and appears spatially concentrated in the top-right region of the tissue.

How do you interpret these observations? Do you think Banksy is providing reliable clusters?

We can also see the relationship between clustering approaches reflected in gene expression patterns across clusters. Below, we’ll examine the expression of Col1a1, a gene we expect to be enriched in tumor-rich spots.

We’ll look up its Ensembl ID to pass to scater::plotExpression():

ensembl_id <- rowData(hvg_spe) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::filter(Symbol == "Col1a1") |>
  rownames()

ensembl_id
[1] "ENSMUSG00000001506"
ENSMUSG00000001506

Now we’ll use scater::plotExpression() to plot Col1a1 expression across non-spatial clusters and Banksy AGF clusters. We’ll also include the coordinate plots again, to assist with interpretation.

# expression across non-spatial clusters
nonspatial_expr_plot <- scater::plotExpression(
  hvg_spe,
  features = ensembl_id,
  x = "cluster_nonspatial",
  color_by = "cluster_nonspatial",
  point_size = 0.5
) +
  scale_color_brewer(name = "Non-spatial cluster", palette = "Dark2")

# expression across AGF clusters
agf_expr_plot <- scater::plotExpression(
  hvg_spe,
  features = ensembl_id,
  x = "cluster_banksy_agf",
  color_by = "cluster_banksy_agf",
  point_size = 0.5
) +
  scale_color_brewer(name = "Banksy AGF cluster", palette = "Paired")


# Compile for plotting with patchwork
plot_list <- list(
  nonspatial_expr_plot,
  agf_expr_plot,
  coords_nonspatial,
  coords_banksky_agf
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot_list, nrow = 2)

Let’s begin interpreting this by focusing on the tumor rich-clusters (3/5 non-spatial and 4, 5 and 7 Banksy AGF). Do these clusters show comparable expression of Cola1a, or do you see distinctions in Cola1a levels? Do you think that the associated Banksy clusters may represent distinct biological regions?

Export

We’ll conclude by exporting the colData slot of the hvg_spe as a TSV, which will include the clusters we have calculated.

# convert colData to data frame and export as a TSV
colData(hvg_spe) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  readr::write_tsv(cluster_tsv)
